ref: Eusebius, Historia ecclesiastica 4.18.4 (book 4, chap. 18, section 4); Greek and English section numbering as in Schwartz/McGiffert
greek: Καὶ παρὰ τού- τς ἄλλο Περὶ Θεοῦ μοναρχίας, ἣν οὐ μόνον ἐχ Ὧν παο᾿ ἡμῖν Γραφῶν, ἀλλὰ χαὶ ἐχ τῶν Ἕλληνι- χῶν συνίστησι βιθλίων
greek_edition: Migne PG 20 (1857), Eusebius HE; archive.org item patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_020 (OCR, not checked against page scan; OCR noise present, e.g. 'τού- τς' for 'τούτοις', 'Ὧν' for 'τῶν', 'χαὶ' for 'καὶ', 'βιθλίων' for 'βιβλίων'). Column number not read.
english: And still another work of his against the Greeks has come down to us, to which he gave the title Refutation. And besides these another, On the Sovereignty of God, which he establishes not only from our Scriptures, but also from the books of the Greeks. 5. Still further, a work entitled Psaltes
translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (NPNF2 vol. 1), as printed on newadvent.org/fathers/250104.htm
page: page unknown (newadvent transcription has no page numbers)
edition: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers 2nd series vol. 1 (Eusebius) - printed text not checked for page
what_it_says: Eusebius lists a work of Justin 'On the Sovereignty of God' (Greek Peri Theou monarchias), proved from scripture and Greek books, and also Refutation, Psaltes and On the Soul; the title matches the pseudo-Justin De monarchia only by name.
use: context (tradition's own catalogue of Justin's works; shows that a lost Justin treatise on divine monarchy existed under that title)
limits: Eusebius gives no text; the title does not prove that the extant De monarchia is the work he names. Eusebius's Greek is from PG 20 OCR.

ref: Eusebius, HE 4.18.9 (quoting Irenaeus, Adv. haer. 4.6.2 and 5.26.2)
greek: κα- λῶς Ἰουστῖνος ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Μαρκίωνα συντάγματί φησιν, ὅτι" Αὐτῷ τῷ Κυρίῳ οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἐπείσθην, ἄλλον Θεὸν χαταγγέλλοντι παρὰ τὸν Δημιουργόν" ν τοῦτο δὲ ἐν τῷ πέμπτῳ τῆς αὐτῆς ὑποθέσεως διὰ τούτων " « Καὶ χαλῶς ὁ Ἰουστῖνος ἔφη, ὅτι πρὸ μὲν τῆς τοῦ Κυρίου παρουσίας οὐδέποτε ἐτόλμησεν ὁ Σατανᾶς βλασφημῆσαι τὸν Θεὸν, ἅτε μηδέπω εἰδὼς αὐτοῦ τὴν χατάχρισιν.
greek_edition: Migne PG 20 (1857), Eusebius HE; archive.org OCR, not checked against scan. This Greek is Eusebius's own rendering of Irenaeus's Latin, not Justin's Greek; OCR noise present (e.g. 'χαταγγέλλοντι', 'χαλῶς', 'χατάχρισιν').
english: And Justin well says in his work against Marcion, that he would not have believed the Lord himself if he had preached another God besides the Creator; and again in the fifth book of the same work he says: And Justin well said that before the coming of the Lord, Satan never dared to blaspheme God, because he did not yet know his condemnation.
translator: Arthur Cushman McGiffert (NPNF2 vol. 1), newadvent.org/fathers/250104.htm
page: page unknown
what_it_says: Eusebius, quoting Irenaeus, reports Justin in his work against Marcion saying he would not have believed the Lord had He announced another God besides the Creator; and that Satan never blasphemed God before the Lord's coming.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Son is not 'another God' in opposition to the Creator)
limits: Second-hand (Irenaeus via Eusebius); the work against Marcion is lost; Irenaeus's Latin is the primary witness (see J11-04, J11-05).

ref: Irenaeus, Adversus haereses 4.6.2 (Greek fragment in Eusebius only; primary text Latin)
greek_edition: Latin original NOT copied (no accessible Latin with a readable text layer; PG 7 archive OCR failed). Greek: none.
english: In his book against Marcion, Justin does well say: I would not have believed the Lord Himself, if He had announced any other than He who is our framer, maker, and nourisher. But because the only-begotten Son came to us from the one God, who both made this world and formed us, and contains and administers all things, summing up His own handiwork in Himself, my faith towards Him is steadfast, and my love to the Father immoveable, God bestowing both upon us.
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1), newadvent.org/fathers/0103406.htm
page: page unknown (newadvent transcription)
what_it_says: Irenaeus cites Justin's work against Marcion: he would not have believed the Lord Himself had He announced any other than the framer, maker and nourisher; the only-begotten Son came from the one God who made the world.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Justin's Son comes from the one Creator God; no second God against the Creator)
limits: Latin not copied; translator's rendering of Irenaeus's Latin, not Justin's Greek; Irenaeus gives no book and section for Justin's work.

ref: Irenaeus, Adversus haereses 5.26.2
greek_edition: Latin original NOT copied. Greek of this sentence exists only in Eusebius HE 4.18.9 (see J11-02).
english: Truly has Justin remarked: That before the Lord's appearance Satan never dared to blaspheme God, inasmuch as he did not yet know his own sentence, because it was contained in parables and allegories; but that after the Lord's appearance, when he had clearly ascertained from the words of Christ and His apostles that eternal fire has been prepared for him as he apostatized from God of his own free-will, and likewise for all who unrepentant continue in the apostasy,
translator: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut (ANF vol. 1), newadvent.org/fathers/0103526.htm
page: page unknown
what_it_says: Irenaeus quotes Justin that before the Lord's appearance Satan never dared to blaspheme God, since he did not yet know his sentence; after the appearance he knew the fire prepared for him.
use: context (Justin's eschatology in Irenaeus's citation; not a Logos passage)
limits: Irenaeus does not name the work by title here; Eusebius attributes it to the work against Marcion.

ref: Jerome, De viris illustribus 23 (Justin Martyr)
greek_edition: Latin original NOT copied (no Latin text with page layer obtained). Jerome gives Greek for one Greek word only (diatribai).
english: Another volume of his Against the nations, is also extant, where he discusses the nature of demons, and a fourth against the nations which he entitled, Refutation and yet another On the sovereignty of God, and another book which he entitled, Psaltes, and another On the Soul
translator: Ernest Cushing Richardson (NPNF2 vol. 3), newadvent.org/fathers/2708.htm
page: page unknown
edition: NPNF2 vol. 3 (Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men)
what_it_says: Jerome lists Justin's works, including 'On the sovereignty of God' and volumes 'Against Marcion', which Irenaeus mentions in book 4 of Against heresies, and 'Against all heresies' mentioned in the Apology.
use: context (later catalogue; confirms the 'On the sovereignty of God' title in the 4th-5th-century tradition)
limits: Jerome copies Eusebius; he does not quote text. Whether 'On the sovereignty of God' is the extant De monarchia is not stated.

ref: Tertullian, Adversus Valentinianos 5 (the chapter 'Many eminent Christian writers...')
greek_edition: Latin original NOT copied.
english: by so many eminently holy and excellent men, not only those who have lived before us, but those also who were contemporary with the heresiarchs themselves: for instance Justin, philosopher and martyr; Miltiades, the sophist of the churches; Irenæus, that very exact inquirer into all doctrines; our own Proculus, the model of chaste old age and Christian eloquence.
translator: Alexander Roberts (ANF vol. 3), newadvent.org/fathers/0314.htm
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 506 (running head read from archive.org djvu OCR 'AGAINST THE VALENTINIANS' with '506'; confirmed on PDF page 520)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (1885 Edinburgh reprint, archive.org antenicenefather03robe)
what_it_says: Tertullian names Justin, 'philosopher and martyr', among the eminent earlier writers who refuted the heresies, along with Miltiades, Irenaeus and Proculus.
use: context (Justin's reputation as a refuter of heresy in the North African tradition)
limits: Says nothing about Justin's doctrine of the Logos; a general praise.

ref: Tertullian, Adversus omnes haereses 7 (ANF heading 'CHAP. VII - TATIAN')
greek_edition: Latin not copied.
english: To all these heretics is added one Tatian, a brother-heretic. This man was Justin Martyr's disciple. After Justin's death he l)egan to cherish different opinions from his.
translator: Rev. S. Thelwall (ANF vol. 3, 'Appendix. Against All Heresies'), as printed in archive.org OCR
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 654 (running head '654 AGAINST ALL HERESIES' before the Tatian heading; confirmed on PDF page 668)
what_it_says: Tatian is 'a brother-heretic' and 'Justin Martyr's disciple', who after Justin's death took different opinions from him.
use: context (the tradition's account of Justin's school; the 'Tatian' break)
limits: OCR error in source: 'l)egan' for 'began' (kept as read in the OCR, corrected here only in this note). Tertullian is the source for the 'disciple' claim; it does not describe Justin's doctrine.

ref: Hippolytus, Refutatio omnium haeresium, ANF 'Chap. XVIII' (system of Justinus; Justinus is a gnostic, not Justin Martyr; standard book/section not verified)
greek_edition: Greek not copied (Hippolytus Greek not checked).
english: Justinus ' was entirely opposed to the teach- ing of the holy Scriptures, and moreover to the written or oral teaching of the blessed evangel- ists, according as the Logos was accustomed to instruct His disciples, saying, " Go not into the way of the Gentiles;"^ and this signifies that they should not attend to the futile doctrine of the Gentiles. This (heretic) endeavours to lead on
translator: Rev. J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5), as printed in archive.org OCR
page: ANF vol. 5 p. 69 (running head '69' before 'CHAP. XVIII')
what_it_says: Hippolytus describes a heretic named Justinus (a Gnostic with a 'Baruch' book) whose system is anti-scriptural; the ANF editor notes that no ecclesiastical history mentions this Justinus.
use: objection (a source of confusion: this 'Justinus' is not Justin Martyr)
limits: The name 'Justinus' is the only link; Hippolytus here does not mention Justin Martyr. Editorial note in ANF: 'No mention occurs of this heretic in ecclesiastical history.'

ref: Hippolytus, Refutatio, ANF 'Chap. IX' (Tatian), after the Monoimus refutation (standard book number not verified)
greek_edition: Greek not copied.
english: Tatian,* however, although being himself a disciple of Justinus the Martyr, did not entertain similar opinions with his master.
translator: Rev. J. H. MacMahon (ANF vol. 5), as printed in archive.org OCR
page: ANF vol. 5, Refutation 'CHAP. IX - TATIAN' (page not read from running head; nearest OCR head unreliable)
what_it_says: Hippolytus says Tatian was a disciple of 'Justinus the Martyr' and did not share his master's opinions.
use: context (the one place where Hippolytus names Justin Martyr as Tatian's teacher; must be kept apart from the heretic Justinus in J11-08)
limits: The text is in ANF's translation; the Greek word for 'Martyr' was not checked; the ANF footnote marks this as a reference.

ref: Pseudo-Justin: works classed as not Justin's (ANF vol. 1 introductory note); De monarchia (De Monarchia), Cohortatio (Hortatory Address), Expositio, Quaestiones
greek_edition: English only (ANF editor's introduction; no Greek).
english: The third class consists of those that are unquestionably not the works of Justin. These are : I. An Exposition of the True Faith; 2. Replies to the Orthodox; 3. Christian Questions to Gentiles; 4. Gentile Questions to Christians; 5. Epistle to Zenas and Serenus ; and 6. A Refu- tation of certain Doctrines of Aristotle. There is no clue to the date of the two last. There can be no doubt that the others were written after the Council of Nicaea, though, immediately after the Reformation, Calvin and others appealed to the first as a genuine writing of Justin
translator: ANF vol. 1 editorial introduction (19th-c. editors; no named translator)
page: ANF vol. 1, Introductory Note to Justin Martyr (OCR running head 'i6i', about p. 161-162)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885 reprint, archive.org antenicenefather01robe)
what_it_says: The ANF editor places the Exposition of the True Faith, Replies to the Orthodox, Christian Questions to Gentiles, Gentile Questions to Christians, Epistle to Zenas and Serenus and Refutation of Aristotle among works 'unquestionably not' Justin's, all written after Nicaea; the Exposition was once cited by Calvin as genuine.
use: answer to objection (a standard way of setting aside the pseudo-Justin texts that critics cite)
limits: This is a 19th-century classification (editors' view). It does not cite the 20th-21st century critical literature, which was not checked.

ref: Pseudo-Justin, De monarchia (On the Sole Government of God), ANF 'Chap. I' (opening); note 'N.B.' by ANF editors
greek_edition: English only; no Greek checked.
english: Although human nature at first received a union of intelligence and safety to discern the truth, and the worship due to the one Lord of all, yet envy, insinuating the excellence of human greatness, turned men away to the making of idols ; and this superstitious custom, after con- tinuing for a long period, is handed down to the majority as if it were natural and true. It is the part of a lover of man, or rather of a lover of God,
translator: Rev. G. Reith, M.A. (ANF vol. 1), as printed in archive.org OCR
page: ANF vol. 1 p. 291 (page per the cross-reference in ANF vol. 2, 'De Monarchia [vol. i. p. 291, this series]')
what_it_says: The work argues for the sole government (monarchia) of God against idols; the ANF editors state that modern critics do not suppose it is Justin's.
use: answer to objection (cannot be used for Justin's doctrine; if Eusebius's lost 'On the Sovereignty of God' (J11-01) is the same title, the extant text is still not shown to be that work)
limits: Authorship is disputed; ANF editors say it is not Justin's; date not fixed in the OCR text.

ref: Bull, Defensio fidei Nicaenae, book III chap. II (Justin's view of the eternity of the Son; answer to Sandius), section 3 (approx.)
greek_edition: English (1851 Oxford ed. of Bull's works, as printed; translator not confirmed). Bull's Latin not copied.
english: He says that Justin taught “that there was a time when that which is begotten did not exist; (than which,” he says, “what comes nearer to the trite saying of the Arians, ‘there was a time when the Son was not ?) that ‘begotten’ and ‘made’ do not differ in reality, but only in word; for every thing which is begotten is made, and vice versa.’ But from this and from many other indications it appears that Sandius has cited testimonies of the ancients either without any judgment, or in despite of conscience’. For first, he has taken the latter statement, * that * begotten’ and ‘made’ do not differ in reality,” from the Questions and Answers to the Greeks” ; a work, which by the consent of all the learned, as Sandius* himself intimates, is decided not to be Justin’s. The former words, “there was a time when that which is begotten did not exist," are found only in the : Confutation of the Opinions of Aristotle, chap. 20; a work; which by the generality of learned men is rejected as spu- rious.
translator: Not confirmed (English text of the 1851 Oxford edition of Bull's Defensio; translator name on title page not read from OCR)
page: PDF p. 56 = printed p. 406 (running head). The passage is on the page headed '406 Sandius's objections'.
edition: Bull, Defensio fidei Nicaenae, 1851 (Oxford), vol. 2; archive.org defensiofideinic02bull
what_it_says: Bull says Sandius quoted Justin as teaching that 'there was a time when that which is begotten did not exist' and that 'begotten' and 'made' do not differ; Bull replies that these words come from pseudo-Justin's Questions and Answers and from a refutation of Aristotle, both spurious, and that they concern the eternity of the world, not the Son.
use: answer to objection (the temporal-generation charge is answered by denying the words are Justin's)
limits: Bull's reply rests on the 17th-century judgement that the Questions and the Aristotle refutation are spurious; Bull's own argument on Justin's 'generation' (Dial. 61-62, 128) is not reproduced here.

ref: Bull, Defensio fidei Nicaenae, book III (Justin on the Son's generation: fire kindled from fire; Dial. 128 passage cited by Bull)
greek_edition: English only (1851 Oxford ed.; translator not confirmed).
english: In these words Justin expressly teaches that the Son is indeed “ numerically another thing,” (apiOu@ ére- pov Ti) another, th
translator: Not confirmed (1851 Oxford edition)
page: printed p. 137-138 (running head '137' precedes the paragraph; not confirmed on a PDF page)
edition: Bull, Defensio fidei Nicaenae, 1851 (Oxford), vol. 1; archive.org defensiofideinic01bull
what_it_says: Bull reads Justin as teaching that the Son is 'numerically another thing' from the Father, as one fire lit from another.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Bull's reading of Justin's numerical distinction, as a Nicene defender)
limits: The English is Bull's translation of Justin's Dial. 128 as summarized by Bull; the Greek is not checked; the OCR cuts the passage short.

ref: Bull, Defensio fidei Nicaenae, book II (citing 'an Exposition of Faith ascribed to Justin', i.e. pseudo-Justin Expositio rectae fidei)
greek_edition: English only (1851 Oxford ed.).
english: And rightly doth the author of a treatise, entitled An Exposition of Faith, (é«0eous miotews,) ascribed to Justin, say
translator: Not confirmed (1851 Oxford edition)
page: page unknown (not located in the OCR)
what_it_says: Bull quotes the 'Exposition of Faith' as Justin's work and uses it for the doctrine that the Son is not a creature.
use: objection (an early-modern appeal to the pseudo-Justin Expositio; ANF editors class it as not Justin's, see J11-10)
limits: Bull treats it as Justin's; the ANF editors say not. The Expositio is therefore not a safe source for Justin's own doctrine.

ref: Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century, ch. II, sect. on the Ecclesiastical Doctrine (Justin's use of 'the Son')
greek_edition: English (Newman's own rendering of Justin, as printed).
english: Thus Justin Martyr speaks of Christ as the Son, " who alone is literally called by that name
translator: John Henry Newman (own translation in The Arians)
page: printed p. 66 (PDF p. 190)
edition: Newman, The Arians of the Fourth Century (1871 ed.), archive.org ariansA2d187100newmuoft
what_it_says: Newman says Justin calls Christ 'the Son' in a sense that is literal of one only; he quotes an argument of Justin (book not identified in Newman's text) that Jesus may be called Son of God from his wisdom.
use: answer to objection (Newman presents this as the ecclesiastical doctrine of the Son, against Arian readings)
limits: Newman's quotation is a paraphrase in translation; the Greek and the chapter of Justin are not given.

ref: Newman quoting Justin: 'second place' (1 Apol. 13 cited by Newman; not verified here)
greek_edition: English (Newman's rendering).
english: Justin, for instance, speaks of the Son as " having the second place after the un changeable and everlasting God and Father of all.
translator: John Henry Newman (own translation)
page: printed p. 70 (PDF p. 194)
what_it_says: Newman cites Justin describing the Son as having 'the second place' after the unchangeable God and Father of all, and treats this as a sign of subordinate order in the Son.
use: objection (Arian-style reading of 'second place'; Newman says it is order of origin, not nature)
limits: Newman's translation; Justin's Greek not checked here (see the main J-items on 1 Apol. 13).

ref: Newman citing Justin, 1 Apol. 63 and Dial. 56
greek_edition: English (Newman's rendering).
english: when Justin speaks of the Son as the minister of God, it is with direct reference to those numerous passages of the Old Testament, in which a ministering angelic presence is more or less characterized by the titles and attributes of Divine Perfection
translator: John Henry Newman (own translation)
page: printed p. 96 (PDF p. 120)
what_it_says: Newman explains Justin's description of the Son as 'minister of God' by reference to Old Testament angelic presences which bear divine titles.
use: answer to objection (Newman's reading of Justin's 'minister' language as angelic/emblematic)
limits: Newman's explanation; not Justin's own argument.

ref: Dial. 62 (cited by Newman in a footnote on 'prolation')
greek_edition: Newman, The Arians (1871), footnote 8, archive.org OCR; Greek as OCR-read (OCR errors likely: 'Λ' and 'ytvvr' letters).
english: Accordingly Justin employed it, or rather a cognate phrase ", to designate what Cyril calls above the self-existence
translator: John Henry Newman (own translation; footnote Greek as printed)
page: printed p. 94 (PDF page not checked)
what_it_says: Newman says Justin used a cognate word for 'prolation' (proboleh) of the Son's generation, cited to Dial. 62, to name the self-existence of the Son.
use: explanation of hard pass (the 'prolation' language of Dial. 62 read by Newman as a Nicene-compatible generation)
limits: Greek is the OCR of Newman's footnote; not checked against Justin's Greek of Dial. 62 (that is an item for the Justin-own passages).

ref: Newman citing Justin, Dial. (the Father is 'cause' of the Son)
greek_edition: English (Newman's rendering; Greek word 'aitios' not confirmed in OCR).
english: The word cause (o,mo?) used in this passage, as a substitute for that use of Origin which peculiarly applies to the Father as the Fount of Divinity, is found as early as the time of Justin Martyr, who in his dialogue with Trypho, declares the Father is to the Son the amo?, or cause of His being ;
translator: John Henry Newman (own translation)
page: printed p. 189 (PDF p. 213)
what_it_says: Newman says Justin declares the Father to be the 'cause' (aitios) of the Son's being, a term the post-Nicene writers later used of the Father's priority.
use: explanation of hard pass (Father as 'cause' of the Son; Newman's reading of Justin's priority language)
limits: The Dial. reference is not given in the OCR text; Greek not checked.

ref: Newman citing Justin, Dial. 61 and 100 (generation referred to the will of God)
greek_edition: English (Newman's rendering).
english: though some suppose that Justin and others referred the divine gennesis or generation to the will of God.
translator: John Henry Newman (own translation)
page: printed p. 201 (PDF p. 225; the text is inside the 'Variations' chapter, not the 198 heading)
what_it_says: Newman says that some suppose Justin and others referred the divine generation of the Son to the will of God, and notes that the Nicene question about generation and will later became subtle.
use: objection (the 'will' language of Dial. 61 and 100 used to support a generation by will)
limits: Newman does not accept the view but reports it ('some suppose'); Justin's own text not checked here.

ref: Newman, Arians, Appendix (on the 'opinion' that the Son is begotten before creation; Justin 2 Apol. 6 cited in the same text)
greek_edition: English (Newman's rendering).
english: The opinion which I have been describing is, as far as words go, definitely held by Justin, Tatian, Theophilus, Methodius, in the East ; by Hippolytus, Tertullian, Nova- tian, Lactantius, Zeno, and Victorinus, in the West ;
translator: John Henry Newman (own translation)
page: printed p. 427 (PDF p. 451)
what_it_says: Newman says the opinion that the Son was generated before the creation of the world is held in identical terms by Justin, Tatian, Theophilus and Methodius in the East and by Hippolytus, Tertullian, Novatian, Lactantius, Zeno and Victorinus in the West.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Newman's list of pre-Nicene witnesses to the pre-creation generation of the Son)
limits: Newman's appendix is a historical claim; the Justin texts behind it are not given in that sentence.
